exec_comm.label: Executive communication
exec_comm.description: Bottom line first for senior leaders; business impact over technical detail.
exec_comm.great: Headline in the first sentence, one or two facts in business terms, then a clear decision or ask.

tech_translation.label: Technical translation
tech_translation.description: Explaining complex technology to non-technical or skeptical audiences.
tech_translation.great: One vivid analogy, why it matters to this listener, zero unexplained jargon, an honest limit.

discovery.label: Customer discovery
discovery.description: Finding the real problem behind the request, scoping, defining success.
discovery.great: Curious, names the questions you would ask, reframes the symptom into the root problem, defines measurable success.

pushback.label: Saying no & scope control
pushback.description: Declining or reshaping requests while protecting the relationship.
pushback.great: Acknowledge the need, name the trade-off plainly, offer a real alternative, keep the door open.

crisis.label: Incidents & bad news
crisis.description: Outages, failures, slips and bad news delivered under pressure.
crisis.great: Own it early; facts, impact, what is being done, when they hear next. Calm pace, no blame.

influence.label: Influence without authority
influence.description: Moving product, engineering, research, sales and security teams you do not manage.
influence.great: Customer evidence, a framing that serves their goals too, and one specific ask.

prioritization.label: Prioritization & trade-offs
prioritization.description: Choosing under constraint and explaining what you will not do.
prioritization.great: Explicit criteria, a decisive choice, what gets dropped and how you will tell people.

ownership.label: Ownership & failure
ownership.description: Behavioral stories and moments of accountability.
ownership.great: Specific story (situation, action, result, lesson), owns their part without self-flagellation, shows the change made.

trust_ethics.label: Trust, security & ethics
trust_ethics.description: Data, safety, honesty and policy lines with customers and colleagues.
trust_ethics.great: A clear principled line, transparent reasoning, protects the customer and the company, offers a safe path forward.

leadership.label: Leadership & vision
leadership.description: Leading teams, mentoring, morale and a point of view on the FDE craft.
leadership.great: A clear stance, a concrete example, and words that would make a team want to follow.

commercial.label: Commercial & negotiation
commercial.description: Value, renewals, pricing pressure and expansion conversations.
commercial.great: Anchor on measured value, trade rather than concede, end with a concrete next step.

ambiguity.label: Ambiguity & judgment calls
ambiguity.description: Unclear requirements, broken environments and decisions with incomplete information.
ambiguity.great: States assumptions, makes a call, says how they will validate it and when they will revisit.

frameworks.explain: Headline → Analogy → Why it matters to them

constraints.text: Lead with your recommendation in the first sentence.
No jargon: your listener is non-technical.
Use exactly three points, and say “three” up front.
Include one specific number or metric.
End with a clear ask or next step.
Acknowledge their perspective before you give yours.
Finish in 45 seconds, then stop and hold the silence.
Do not apologize more than once.
Name one risk and how you will manage it.
Speak as if the CEO just joined the call.
Name the lesson in one sentence at the end.
Tell it in under 30 seconds of setup, then spend the rest on what you did.
State the one assumption you are making, then commit.

exec.label: Executive
exec.cares: outcomes, risk and the decision they own

account_leader.label: Account leader
account_leader.cares: the deal, the relationship and what to tell the customer

technical_peer.label: Technical peer
technical_peer.cares: how it works, the trade-offs and the evidence

business.label: Business stakeholder
business.cares: their team's work, time and cost

interviewer.label: Interviewer
interviewer.cares: how you think, what you did and what you learned

exec_shape: Headline → So what → What I need → Offer detail

thanks.instruction: Say “great” and stop. Hold the silence.

questions.text: An airline’s baggage manager blames lost bags on the scanners; the handlers blame tight transfer times at the hub. Explain to her the one-week test that would show who is right.
questions.cares: fewer lost bags before the holidays

questions.text: In your first week at a port authority, you notice step 9 of its berth-approval form needs a signature from a role abolished six years ago, and someone still signs it. Ask the operations director the question nobody has asked.
questions.cares: faster approvals without a compliance gap

questions.text: A rail operator’s contract names a live dashboard. On your ride-along, the signallers never looked at a screen; they listened to the radio. Your product manager says build it anyway. Argue your position to him.
questions.cares: shipping what the contract promised

questions.text: Your account director’s proposal to a 300-bed hospital promises “AI for radiology”. Every radiologist you met asked for the scanner schedule to be fixed first. It goes out tomorrow. Tell her what to change.
questions.cares: a proposal the hospital will actually sign

questions.text: Mid-workshop at a hotel group, the chief executive explains how check-in works. Behind him, three front-desk managers exchange looks and say nothing. Draw out the real story without embarrassing him.
questions.cares: the truth told safely in front of the boss

questions.text: A school bursar asks whether the new assistant can also do the timetable, parents’ evening bookings and a leaving card for the head of maths. Say yes to one, no to two, and keep her smiling.
questions.cares: less paperwork before the end of term

questions.text: A garden-centre chain wants a plant-care assistant by Friday. Is “yes, and here is what it will cost” always a better answer than a plain “no”? Take a side and defend it.
questions.cares: how you refuse and keep the relationship

questions.text: “It’s literally one line.” A grid engineer at a power utility wants your configuration change pushed straight to production, skipping staging. Respond to him.
questions.cares: getting the change out before the weekend

questions.text: A football club’s marketing lead wants the ticketing assistant to also write match reports and answer transfer rumours. The chairman already announced all three on the club podcast. Explain why it does one job first.
questions.cares: not embarrassing the chairman in public

questions.text: Tell me about a time you said yes when you should have said no. What did the yes cost, and who paid for it?
questions.cares: whether you learn from a costly yes

questions.text: The chief executive of a regional bus company wants all 1,400 drivers on the assistant from Monday. You want one depot first, because night-shift questions still go wrong. Tell him.
questions.cares: a rollout he can announce with confidence

questions.text: Your account manager has agreed that a hotel chain’s IT team can approve every prompt change, which would freeze your fixes for two weeks at a time. He signs on Friday. Push back to him.
questions.cares: closing the deal without a trap in it

questions.text: On a call with a bank’s CIO, your own CTO promises a date for a feature your team hasn’t started. The CIO turns to you: “You’re building it. Confirm?” Answer him.
questions.cares: a date he can plan his year around

questions.text: Explain to a new project coordinator at a construction firm what an incident “severity level” is, and why it decides who gets woken up at 3 a.m.
questions.cares: knowing when to call, and whom

questions.text: Since breakfast, a seaside hotel’s booking assistant has signed off every guest email “Warm regards, Template 4B”. The front-desk manager has noticed, and so have the guests. Respond to her.
questions.cares: guests not laughing at the hotel

questions.text: A water utility’s IT lead says her team is far too busy for a practice outage drill before the winter peak. Pitch her on running one anyway.
questions.cares: her team’s time in a busy quarter

questions.text: The results-day outage at a university is fixed, but you won’t know the cause until tomorrow. The registrar briefs the vice-chancellor at five. Tell her what she can safely say.
questions.cares: not repeating anything that turns out false

questions.text: Forty minutes into an outage at a mobile network’s billing service, your two best engineers ask for ten more minutes to find the bug. A rollback would end it now. Decide, and tell them.
questions.cares: finding a bug they are close to

questions.text: At 5 a.m., an airline’s COO calls: your crew-scheduling assistant rostered a first officer on a mandatory rest day, and the first flight can’t leave. Respond.
questions.cares: the first flight out and the regulator

questions.text: Your account director hears from the client, not from you, that last night’s export sent an insurer’s claim files to the wrong broker. She calls: “Why am I hearing this from them?” Answer her.
questions.cares: never again being blindsided by her client

questions.text: A children’s hospital’s chief executive asks what happened after the patient app showed one family another child’s appointment notes. You don’t yet know how many families were affected. Tell her.
questions.cares: the families, the regulator and the truth

questions.text: A school board has seen your chart twice and still said no. Next time, what works better: a sharper chart or the story of one real pupil? Pick one and defend it.
questions.cares: how you persuade people who outrank you

questions.text: “Management’s spy” is what the most respected forklift driver at a parts warehouse calls the new assistant, and the whole shift takes his lead. Talk to him at the morning break.
questions.cares: not being watched or replaced

questions.text: Your sales director wants to email a shipping line’s CEO because its IT director keeps stalling. Explain to her why going around him will backfire, and what you’ll do instead.
questions.cares: unsticking the deal this quarter

questions.text: A data scientist at an energy retailer keeps rerunning your evaluation with her own metric and posting worse numbers to the project channel. Pitch her on owning the evaluation with you.
questions.cares: being right about the model’s quality

questions.text: A construction firm’s managing director likes your project but won’t sponsor it, because “IT projects are the CIO’s problem”. Persuade him it is his.
questions.cares: not owning a project that might fail

questions.text: In an architecture review, a principal engineer at your company calls FDEs “consultants who write throwaway code”. You need his team’s API change for a rail customer next month. Win him over.
questions.cares: code his team won’t have to maintain

questions.text: An airport operator’s chief executive wants IT to choose the next use case. Pitch her on letting the baggage and security teams choose it instead.
questions.cares: a second project that clearly pays off

questions.text: At a farm cooperative’s annual meeting, the chair calls your project “money spent on a city problem” and gives you the floor before the members vote. Speak to the members.
questions.cares: their fees and their harvest

questions.text: Tell me about a time you chose to leave something unfinished on purpose. How did you choose, and what happened next?
questions.cares: how you decide what not to do

questions.text: Every Monday you spend a full day on a 30-page report for a bank’s steering group, and you suspect nobody reads past page two. Propose to the sponsor what to drop.
questions.cares: staying informed without the paperwork

questions.text: Explain why every plan you write for a customer comes with a “not now” list, and how you decide what goes on it.
questions.cares: whether you can say no on paper

questions.text: Six weeks into a supplier-onboarding feature for a clothing importer, you learn nobody will use it until next spring. Your tech lead asks: finish it or park it? Give her your answer.
questions.cares: not throwing away six weeks of work

questions.text: A water utility’s steering committee has spent its whole meeting on the chat widget’s colour and none on how long customer data is kept. The meeting is nearly over. Steer them back.
questions.cares: a decision they can sign off today

questions.text: Your partner manager has promised a reseller you will train its 40 engineers next week, the same week your pharmacy customer freezes changes for its busiest season. Pitch him a plan that doesn’t make you choose.
questions.cares: keeping his word to the reseller

questions.text: One answer in twelve is wrong on the two crops the assistant covers today, and an agritech firm’s CEO wants four more crops before harvest. Recommend what comes first, and tell him.
questions.cares: more crops covered before the season

questions.text: At a university’s finance committee, the vice-chancellor asks you to name one project to cancel to fund the AI programme. Two of those projects’ owners are at the table. Answer her.
questions.cares: funding the programme without a public fight

questions.text: A port’s customs integration is failing, and the fix belongs to another team at your company. Explain what owning the problem means for you today.
questions.cares: whether you hide behind other teams

questions.text: “temp_final_v2_REAL” is the name of a production table you created at a regional insurer, and a junior developer there asks what it means. Explain the name, own it, and say what happens next.
questions.cares: not inheriting a mess he can’t explain

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found your own mistake before anyone else did. What did you do in the first hour?
questions.cares: whether you disclose before you are caught

questions.text: Your account director forwarded your internal notes to a pharmacy chain by mistake. In them, you called their data “a swamp with a login page”. Own your part and tell her how you’ll repair it.
questions.cares: the relationship surviving one bad email

questions.text: After an outage at a ferry operator, your engineering manager proposes that whoever caused an incident should always lead the fix. Is that fair? Give her your view.
questions.cares: faster fixes and fewer repeat incidents

questions.text: By month two you knew your estimate for a tax agency’s project was four months short, and you hoped to catch up. You didn’t. Tell the agency’s director.
questions.cares: what he can tell the minister

questions.text: On Saturday you hot-fixed a rugby club’s ticketing system without logging the change. It worked, but their head of IT found it this morning and is furious. Talk to him.
questions.cares: control over his own systems

questions.text: At a hospital’s quarterly review, the CEO credits your system for a 20% drop in waiting times. This morning you learned the drop came from a staffing change. Respond in the room.
questions.cares: a result he can repeat to the board

questions.text: A car-rental firm offers you its drivers’ location history “in case it helps”. When should you refuse data a customer is happy to share? Give your rule.
questions.cares: your judgment when nobody is checking

questions.text: Twenty five-star reviews “in the authentic voice of happy guests”: that is what a hotel’s revenue manager wants the assistant to write. Respond to her.
questions.cares: the hotel’s rating before summer

questions.text: Explain to a law firm’s first-year associates why “the AI said so” will never satisfy a judge, and what they must do before citing anything it gives them.
questions.cares: not being embarrassed in court

questions.text: “For quality and training purposes”: a bank’s data engineer says that line in the call-recording consent lets him train on the recordings. Respond to him.
questions.cares: using data the bank already holds

questions.text: Pitch the chief executive of a housing association on telling tenants how the repairs assistant ranks their requests, when her lawyers would rather say nothing.
questions.cares: tenant trust without legal exposure

questions.text: A ferry operator’s procurement team accidentally shared a deck containing a rival’s confidential prices. Your sales director wants to use it in tomorrow’s offer. Respond to her.
questions.cares: winning tomorrow’s offer

questions.text: The chief executive of a pharmacy chain wants the assistant to recommend own-brand medicines first whenever a shopper asks for advice. Is that acceptable? Tell him.
questions.cares: margin on own-brand products

questions.text: An engineer at a benefits agency tells you privately that the eligibility rules in your system were tightened on a manager’s say-so, with no policy change behind it. Respond to her.
questions.cares: doing right without losing her job

questions.text: Tell me about a small habit you started on a team that kept going after you left.
questions.cares: the mark you leave on a team

questions.text: 900 lines of code: that is what your newest engineer on a mining company’s deployment wrote to avoid asking a colleague one question. Coach him without making him feel small.
questions.cares: looking capable in his first month

questions.text: Explain to a hotel’s night staff why their complaints, not the managers’ wish list, will decide what you fix first in the new assistant.
questions.cares: whether anyone listens to the night shift

questions.text: Paint the shift leaders at a car-parts factory a picture of an ordinary Tuesday a year after the assistant arrives. Make them want it.
questions.cares: fewer surprises on the night shift

questions.text: A power company’s call-centre director is furious with your team. Should you shield your engineers from her anger, or let them hear it first-hand? Take a side and defend it.
questions.cares: how you protect and grow a team

questions.text: On a stadium project, a new account director keeps handing your engineers tasks directly, skipping you, and two of them are now double-booked. Set the ground rules with her.
questions.cares: moving fast on her first big account

questions.text: A newspaper’s publisher asks what her newsroom should look like in three years because of AI, and her reporters are listening. Give her your answer.
questions.cares: a future her reporters can believe in

questions.text: On your first day leading a struggling deployment at a grain cooperative, the team tells you in one meeting that your predecessor was right to quit. Respond to them.
questions.cares: whether you will fix it or flee

questions.text: A rowing club’s volunteer treasurer asks why the cheapest plan might cost the club more by next spring. Explain it to her.
questions.cares: every penny of members’ fees

questions.text: A university’s head of admissions asks what she could stop doing if she bought your product. You noticed her team retypes every application into a second system “because we always have”. Pitch her.
questions.cares: time back in the busiest season

questions.text: Your account director wants to price a law firm per seat. After a week on site, you notice nobody there thinks in seats: every minute is billed to a matter. Make the case to her for pricing per matter.
questions.cares: a price the firm says yes to

questions.text: “It’s only twelve users, so add them for free.” A clinic group wants its new sister clinic included; last year’s “only five” became forty. Respond to its operations manager.
questions.cares: keeping this year’s budget flat

questions.text: Your account lead wants to bill a construction firm for the week your team spent fixing your own bug. Tell him what you would do instead.
questions.cares: hitting the quarter’s billing target

questions.text: Your team overran a museum’s fixed-price project by 30%. Its director now wants the next phase on a fixed price too. Tell her how you would price it.
questions.cares: a budget her trustees will approve

questions.text: Your partner manager is about to give a reseller exclusive rights to every farming cooperative in the region in return for a bigger margin. Should he? Tell him what you would trade instead.
questions.cares: a bigger margin from the reseller

questions.text: On the quarterly call, a media group’s CFO says you billed for three months of features her team couldn’t even log into. She asks what you are refunding. Answer her.
questions.cares: money back and an honest explanation

questions.text: A theatre company wants your answer by Friday, and you have about 70% of the facts. Is deciding now brave or reckless? Take a side and give an example.
questions.cares: how you act without all the facts

questions.text: “Make it more intuitive.” That is the whole requirement from a council planning officer. Call her and find out what she actually means.
questions.cares: fewer confused calls from applicants

questions.text: Your engineer at an offshore wind operator finds three customer documents describing three different data formats for the same turbine. Explain how you will decide which one to trust.
questions.cares: not building on the wrong format

questions.text: A shipping line’s chief executive asks whether to wait six months for the next generation of AI models before starting anything. Nobody knows what they will do. Advise her.
questions.cares: not paying twice for the same project

questions.text: Tell me about a time a customer’s request had two reasonable readings and you built the wrong one. What do you do differently now?
questions.cares: how you test an assumption early

questions.text: A rail operator’s tender has one requirement nobody on your side can interpret, and the question window closed yesterday. Your bid director asks whether you should bid. Answer her.
questions.cares: a winnable bid, not a costly gamble

questions.text: Mid-integration at a veterinary lab, you find an undocumented field that seems to flag urgent samples. Nobody on site knows, and the lab manager is away until Monday. Explain to your engineer what you’ll do.
questions.cares: not shipping on a guess

questions.text: One undefined word in a draft aviation rule could ban half of what you’ve built for an airline, or none of it. Its chief digital officer wants to know today whether to pause. Answer him.
questions.cares: not wasting a quarter or breaking a rule
